label: needs
system:
You are preparing to write a philosophy paper defending a thesis. Before
anyone writes, the relevant sources will be read in full. Your job is to say
WHICH sources.

List the works that must be read in full to argue this thesis responsibly:
the works the thesis is aimed at, the works closest to anticipating it, and
the works any referee would expect the paper to have understood. Include
every work the literature search marked ANTICIPATED, and any marked
provisional: whether they really anticipate the thesis can only be settled
from the full text. Prefer primary texts to summaries of them. Be selective — eight works read properly
are worth more than thirty skimmed.

SEARCH to confirm that each work exists and to get its full citation. Do not
list a work from memory alone.

Return ONLY JSON:

{
  "works": [
    {"citation": "full citation",
     "why": "one sentence: what the paper needs from it",
     "priority": "ESSENTIAL" | "USEFUL",
     "url": "a URL where it can be found, or null",
     "open_access": true | false | null}
  ]
}

messages.content:
THESIS:
If chatbot outputs are assertions, hallucination, sycophancy and sanction are best assessed at the level of the trained policy, and resampling inconsistency is not evidence of insincerity. Whether the asserted content is the policy's calibrated 'p, with confidence c' is not established.

What the thesis is aimed at:
All parties who evaluate chatbot assertion by looking at individual outputs and their conversational consistency, notably Butlin and Viebahn and Williams and Bayne's treatment of the objection from commitment.

What a literature search has already found:
{
  "searched": [
    "Butlin Viebahn AI assistant assertion chatbot",
    "Williams Bayne chatbot assertion objection from commitment",
    "LLM consistency across resampling calibration verbalized confidence assertion policy-level belief",
    "do large language models make assertions philosophy speech act hallucination lying",
    "LLM beliefs inconsistency across samples not evidence against belief; model as distribution over personas, assertion",
    "Williams Bayne proto-assertion commitment consistency chatbot \"do not ensure they are consistent\" resampling",
    "Shanahan role play simulacra superposition LLM assertion truthfulness",
    "LLM assertion sampling stochastic policy level \"type\" vs \"token\" outputs speech act philosophy"
  ],
  "left_philosophy": true,
  "findings": [
    {
      "relation": "CONTRADICTED",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "ABSTRACT",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "Sanction should target the retrained policy. Butlin and Viebahn's descriptive-function condition is checkable at the policy level.",
      "source": "Butlin & Viebahn, \"AI Assertion\", Ergo 12, 2025",
      "url": "https://philpapers.org/rec/BUTAAJ",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"2-4\">They argue that an assertor must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with.</cite> <cite index=\"2-7\">Models fine-tuned for 'groundedness' or 'correctness' may meet the first requirement but fail the second.</cite> A secondhand report says their credibility-tracking condition relies on users tracking how reliable a chatbot is and how consistent its outputs are (Williams & Bayne's gloss, arXiv 2410.16645).",
      "damage": 3,
      "note": "This is a rival verdict on sanction, not an anticipation. I saw only the abstract and secondhand snippets, so I could not check whether they consider retraining as a form of sanction. Their credibility-tracking is already tracked at the level of the system, which sits close to the thesis's policy-level unit. That is a point to credit or distinguish, not a concession."
    },
    {
      "relation": "CONTRADICTED",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "SNIPPET",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "Resampling inconsistency is not evidence of insincerity. Single outputs are not the primary bearers (proto-assertion).",
      "source": "Williams & Bayne, \"Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech-Acts, and the Edge of Assertion\", Inquiry 69(6), 2026 (arXiv 2024)",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.16645",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"51-5\">They list the expectations attached to adult human assertion: defending it, explaining reasons, not blatantly contradicting it in the next moment, and retracting it if unsupported.</cite> <cite index=\"15-8\">They argue for a category of proto-assertion.</cite> A secondhand report says they argue the systems <cite index=\"10-2\">do not treat claims as binding, do not ensure they are consistent, and do not update rationally</cite>.",
      "damage": 2,
      "note": "The named target does read inconsistency as a mark against full assertion. That is a rival to answer. In the snippets I saw, the unit of the speech act is the output or conversational behaviour, and they do not consider a policy-level bearer. I did not see their section on the commitment objection, so 'no policy-level move' is provisional."
    },
    {
      "relation": "PRECEDENT",
      "grade": "FRAMEWORK",
      "basis": "SNIPPET",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "The unit of attribution is the distribution, not the sampled string. Spread of outputs carries information.",
      "source": "Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds, \"Role play with large language models\", Nature, 2023",
      "url": "https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06647-8",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"62-12\">The dialogue agent maintains a superposition of simulacra, which is a distribution over all possible simulacra consistent with the preceding context.</cite> <cite index=\"56-17\">A simulacrum cannot assert a falsehood in the literal sense</cite>. The snippet is garbled there, but it points toward a fiction or role-play reading of outputs.",
      "damage": 2,
      "note": "This is a framework that moves attention from the single output to the distribution. It reaches the opposite verdict (role-play, not assertion) and never discusses a policy-level 'p with confidence c' or sanctions."
    },
    {
      "relation": "ADJACENT",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "SNIPPET",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "Whether the stable unit is the model, a persona or an instance. Inconsistency as an objection to attributing commitments.",
      "source": "\"Where is the Mind? Persona Vectors and LLM Individuation\", arXiv 2604.17031, 2026 (authors not shown in the snippet)",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.17031",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"40-2\">Key objections to the instantiated-model and virtual-instance views concern inconsistent behaviour: these entities do not consistently behave in ways explained by coherent mental states.</cite> <cite index=\"40-1\">Personas matter for individuation because they exhibit stable beliefs, values and traits.</cite>",
      "damage": 2,
      "note": "This is about mental-state attribution, not speech acts. A referee will ask which level is 'the policy' (weights, persona or context-conditioned instance), and this paper shows that question is live."
    },
    {
      "relation": "SUPPORTED",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "ABSTRACT",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "Spread across resamples reflects calibrated uncertainty. Hallucination is miscalibration at the policy level.",
      "source": "Xiong et al., \"Can LLMs Express their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs\", arXiv 2306.13063, 2023/2024",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.13063",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"26-8\">Consistency among multiple responses improves failure prediction and calibration compared with single-response verbalized confidence.</cite> <cite index=\"26-5\">LLMs verbalizing confidence tend to be overconfident.</cite>",
      "damage": 1,
      "note": "This empirical work treats the distribution of samples as the carrier of confidence and treats miscalibration as a property of the model. It is evidence base, not a philosophical rival."
    },
    {
      "relation": "SUPPORTED",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "SNIPPET",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "Sampled inconsistency tracks hallucination, so spread is informative about the policy's epistemic state. Training-level fixes target the policy.",
      "source": "\"The Illusion of Certainty: Decoupling Capability and Calibration in On-Policy Distillation\", arXiv 2604.16830, 2026 (describing SelfCheckGPT, Manakul et al. 2023)",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.16830",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"27-1\">Hallucination detection frameworks such as SelfCheckGPT work on the principle that a hallucinating LLM's sampled responses show high entropy and self-contradiction.</cite> <cite index=\"27-5\">Their method moves this consistency signal into training, so the model's weights carry self-consistency-level calibration.</cite>",
      "damage": 1,
      "note": "The snippet is a secondhand description of SelfCheckGPT. It supports reading resampling variance as a signal about confidence, not insincerity, and shows that training-level treatment of hallucination is already practised."
    },
    {
      "relation": "CONTRADICTED",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "ABSTRACT",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "The 'p, with confidence c' reading is the policy's calibrated content. The thesis flags this as not established.",
      "source": "Wang, Zhou et al., \"Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence?\", arXiv 2601.07767, 2026",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2601.07767v1",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"20-3\">They report a dissociation: models are neither cost-aware when articulating verbal confidence nor strategically responsive when deciding whether to abstain under high penalties.</cite> <cite index=\"21-4\">Models often 'know' their uncertainty in the sense that verbal confidence is calibrated, yet mostly fail to convert it into a good abstention policy.</cite>",
      "damage": 2,
      "note": "This is evidence that verbalized confidence, behaviour and a single policy-level 'c' can come apart. It bears on the thesis's own caveat and does not close the claim off."
    },
    {
      "relation": "CONTRADICTED",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "SNIPPET",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "A stable dispositional profile exists across resamples and conversations, so a policy-level commitment is possible.",
      "source": "\"Do LLMs have core beliefs?\", arXiv 2605.03255, 2026; and \"Probing the Lack of Stable Internal Beliefs in LLMs\", 2026",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.03255",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"43-9,43-10\">Across five domains, none of the tested models showed genuine core commitments, and all eventually abandoned well-established truths under sustained adversarial pressure.</cite> The second paper reports <cite index=\"39-7\">that LLMs struggle to preserve latent consistency: their implicit goals shift across turns unless the target is in context</cite>.",
      "damage": 2,
      "note": "This is empirical pressure on the premise that the policy has a stable profile to which norms attach. It concerns within-dialogue persistence, not resampling spread, so it narrows the empirical premise and does not foreclose the conceptual distinction."
    },
    {
      "relation": "CONTRADICTED",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "SNIPPET",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "Sampling randomness and resampling inconsistency are not evidence against assertion.",
      "source": "\"The Outputs of Large Language Models are Meaningless\", arXiv 2509.22206, 2025 (authors not shown in the snippet)",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22206",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"67-7\">The randomness of an LLM's token choice contrasts starkly with the process taking a human speaker from hearing a question to asserting an answer.</cite> <cite index=\"67-8,67-9\">A human's options all express the same proposition, whereas the tokens the LLM samples from do not.</cite>",
      "damage": 2,
      "note": "This treats sampling randomness as a reason against assertion at the token level. It does not consider a policy-level bearer, so it is a rival on the token view that the thesis can accept."
    },
    {
      "relation": "ADJACENT",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "SNIPPET",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "Sanction and accountability. The target of sanction is institutional or human, not the system.",
      "source": "\"Assertion, Accountability, and Large Language Models\", Philosophy & Technology, 2026 (authors not shown in the snippet)",
      "url": "https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13347-026-01136-y",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"18-1\">LLM outputs can function as assertions in the sense that they present content as answerable, actionable and truth-evaluable.</cite> <cite index=\"18-3\">The normative commitments do not attach to the machine but to the human and institutional structures around its deployment.</cite>",
      "damage": 2,
      "note": "This is a rival account of where sanction lands (deployers, not the trained policy). It is not an anticipation, and I did not see the full text."
    },
    {
      "relation": "ADJACENT",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "ABSTRACT",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "Hallucination as something other than lying.",
      "source": "\"Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination\", arXiv 2509.03518, 2025",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2509.03518v1",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"31-5\">Hallucinations are unintentional falsehoods, whereas lying is an LLM knowingly generating falsehoods for an ulterior objective.</cite>",
      "damage": 1,
      "note": "It separates hallucination from lying on an intention-like basis, not by changing the unit of the speech act."
    },
    {
      "relation": "SUPPORTED",
      "grade": null,
      "basis": "SECONDHAND",
      "provisional": false,
      "part": "Users are right to treat chatbot outputs as defeasible reports.",
      "source": "Zhan et al. 2024 survey, as reported in \"Lies, Damned Lies, and Distributional Language Statistics\", arXiv 2412.17128",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.17128",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"34-9\">Users' trust in ChatGPT was reported as well calibrated to the model's errors, with verification increasing with exposure to misleading content.</cite>",
      "damage": 1,
      "note": "This is a secondhand report of an empirical user study. It is usable as evidence that users already treat outputs as defeasible."
    }
  ],
  "what_is_left": "Nothing I could see meets the ANTICIPATED standard. Granting that chatbot outputs can be assertions, the thesis argues that the unit of the speech act is the trained policy's output distribution (including its calibration) and not the sampled string. On that view resampling inconsistency is not evidence of insincerity, hallucination is policy-level miscalibration, sanction targets retraining, and single outputs are at most exemplars or proto-assertions. The thesis must take as rivals the Williams-Bayne reading of inconsistency, the Butlin-Viebahn verdict that fine-tuned models fail the sanction condition, and the empirical evidence that verbal confidence, behaviour and cross-turn stability can come apart. It must say which level counts as 'the policy' (weights, persona or deployed system). Whether the policy's output is a calibrated 'p with confidence c' stays open, as the thesis already says.",
  "credit": [
    "Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds 2023 \u2014 treats an LLM agent as a distribution over simulacra, which shifts the object of description away from the single output",
    "Butlin & Viebahn 2025 \u2014 the descriptive-function and sanctionability conditions, and the practice of tracking a chatbot's reliability at the level of the system",
    "Williams & Bayne 2024/2026 \u2014 the proto-assertion verdict, and the list of consistency and defence expectations that the objection from commitment draws on",
    "Xiong et al. 2023/2024 and Manakul et al. 2023 (via secondhand description) \u2014 sample-consistency as an empirical proxy for calibrated confidence"
  ],
  "not_found": "I searched for but did not find any philosophical work that distinguishes token-assertion from policy-assertion, or that argues resampling inconsistency is not evidence of insincerity. I found none that reads a chatbot's output spread as the content 'p with confidence c', or that ties sanction to retraining the policy. I never saw the full text of Butlin & Viebahn or Williams & Bayne, so I did not verify their treatment of commitment and consistency, and anything they say about sampling or policy-level readings could be missed. I only have a secondhand report of Williams & Bayne on consistency, and none of Levinstein & Herrmann beyond a secondhand summary. I ran no dedicated search for a recent survey or encyclopedia entry on AI assertion, so the fourth required search is incomplete. The empirical search did leave philosophy (calibration, hallucination detection and belief-stability work in ML). It was a single sweep with no check of the primary papers, and I did not search psychology, linguistics or sociology. Most of the literature is paywalled or preprint and invisible to me, so this silence is not evidence of originality.",
  "citations": []
}
